planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger passes in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; give Phoenix a trellis or fence, since it climbs several feet when supported.

directions: Sow directly in lean, well-drained soil, since overly rich ground produces lush foliage but fewer flowers. Phoenix is a nineteenth-century heirloom distinguished by its unusual split, flame-like petals that flare into three or four pointed lobes rather than the rounded shape typical of most nasturtiums, in a mix of crimson, gold, orange, and cream often brushed with copper at the base. Train the climbing stems up a trellis or let them scramble through a fence for the best display of the unusual blooms. Flowers and young leaves are edible with a peppery bite, and the plant flowers continuously through summer into fall until frost.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-10 weeks before last frost, or sow directly in late summer for fall and winter bloom in mild climates; this reliable heirloom self-sows readily once established.

directions: Sow seed and cover lightly, since light aids germination; keep the seedbed cool and evenly moist. Helen Mount is a classic, widely grown Johnny-jump-up strain bearing small flowers that combine purple, lavender-blue, and yellow in the familiar tricolor pattern, held just above a low, spreading mound of foliage. It blooms from early spring through fall in cool climates and self-sows freely, often returning as a welcome volunteer in gravel paths and border edges for years afterward. The edible flowers make a cheerful, mildly flavored garnish for salads, desserts, and drinks.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or propagate named stock from cuttings or division, since seed-grown plants can vary; Molly Sanderson is most often sold as a perennial plant for reliable true-to-type black flowers.

directions: Grow in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade where summers are hot. Molly Sanderson is a hardy, spreading perennial viola holding an RHS Award of Garden Merit, prized for its velvety, near-black flowers lit only by a small yellow eye and faint white markings on the lower petal, an especially striking near-black among garden flowers. It flowers over a long season from spring into summer and again in fall where summers are mild, and shearing plants back lightly after the first flush encourages repeat bloom. The edible flowers make a dramatic dark garnish for pale desserts and drinks.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Viola 'Molly Sanderson' AGM

planting.note: Most often grown from divisions or nursery plants rather than seed, since named Violetta group selections do not come true from seed; set out in early spring or fall in cool, moist, well-drained soil.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, with some morning sun for best flowering. Rebecca is a compact member of the fragrant Violetta group of violas, bearing small creamy-white flowers flushed pale lemon at the center and irregularly flecked with violet-mauve toward the petal edges, backed by a light, sweet fragrance unusual among violas. It forms a tidy mounding clump of evergreen foliage and flowers heavily in spring with a lighter repeat in fall. The edible flowers add a delicate, faintly sweet garnish to salads and desserts, and clumps are easily divided every few years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for fall and winter bloom in mild climates; Art Shades flowers most heavily in cool weather and slows in summer heat.

directions: Direct sow shallowly in average, well-drained soil in full sun; calendula tolerates poor soil but blooms best with regular moisture. Art Shades is a tall, long-stemmed mixed strain carrying large double and semi-double flowers in warm, romantic tones of cream, peach, apricot, and soft orange, many with a darker mahogany flush at the petal tips or center that sets it apart from solid-colored calendula mixes. The long stems make it a good cutting-garden choice, and the edible petals carry the tangy, faintly resinous flavor typical of pot marigold, good scattered fresh over salads or dried for tea. Deadhead every few days to keep the show going and reduce self-sowing if a tidy bed is the goal.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for fall bloom; Flashback Mix tolerates light frost and keeps flowering into the cool of autumn.

directions: Sow directly in average, well-drained soil in full sun; calendula is unfussy about soil but flowers best with consistent moisture. Flashback Mix takes its name from the muted burgundy undersides of its petals, which flash into view each evening as the double and semi-double flowers close, contrasting with the orange, apricot, peach, and cream tones on the upper face. Plants are notably frost-tolerant for a calendula, extending the bloom season later into fall than many other strains. Harvest flowers as they open for the strongest flavor and color in salads, rice dishes, and baked goods, and deadhead regularly to prolong bloom.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall crop; Neon's tall stems and vivid color hold up well as a cut flower.

directions: Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, watering regularly during bloom for the best flower size. Neon bears fully double, brilliant orange flowers edged in a glowing burnt-umber reverse, a more saturated and ultra-double form than older calendula strains, held on tall, sturdy stems well suited to cutting. It flowers continuously from spring through the first hard frosts, outlasting many other annuals in the fall garden. The petals carry the characteristic tangy, saffron-like flavor of pot marigold and can be used fresh in salads or dried for tea; deadhead regularly to keep new buds coming.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant 7-10 weeks before first fall frost for the most reliable heads, since spring sowings are prone to bolting as days lengthen.

directions: Direct sow or set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping moisture consistent for fast, uninterrupted growth. Minuet is a compact mini napa cabbage forming dense, upright heads only about 9 inches tall, with dark green outer leaves wrapping a sweet, pale yellow interior, making it a good fit for small households or closer spacing than standard-size napa types. It holds well in the field without splitting and resists tipburn and bottom rot better than many older varieties. Harvest when heads feel firm when squeezed, and store trimmed heads refrigerated for use in kimchi, stir-fries, and soups.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant 10-12 weeks before first fall frost; Monument is a mid-season type best grown as a fall crop, since its longer maturity window leaves more time for spring bolting.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, with steady moisture to support the long, narrow heads through their extended growing season. Monument is a mid-season napa cabbage forming tall, narrow, densely wrapped heads rather than the broader barrel shapes of many faster-maturing types, with crisp, mild-flavored leaves well suited to kimchi, hot pot, and long storage. Because it takes longer to mature than types like Minuet or Bilko, timing a fall sowing early enough is important so heads finish well before hard frost. Harvest when heads are firm and tight, and store trimmed heads refrigerated for several weeks to months.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Brassica rapa Pekinensis Group

planting.note: Direct sow 3-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, and again 6-8 weeks before first fall frost; this traditional strain germinates and establishes reliably in cold soil.

directions: Scatter seed thinly over fertile, well-drained soil and cover lightly, keeping the bed evenly moist for fast, even germination. Early Mizuna is a traditional strain originating in the mountainous Kyoto region of Japan, prized for its particularly fast growth and strong cold tolerance even during germination, which allows sowing earlier in spring than most other mizuna types. It forms a loose rosette of deeply cut, feathery, mild-flavored leaves that can be cut young for salad mixes or allowed to grow larger for stir-fries and hot pot. Harvest by cutting the whole rosette an inch above the soil for quick regrowth, or pick outer leaves continuously; flavor stays mild and peppery without the bitterness that heat-stressed plants can develop.
